annotation: Emoji are register markers from another medium. In governed technical prose, they add tone where calibrated language already fixes tone (§5.6, P2). A regular expression can perform the check.

title: No canned section formulas
before: "Despite its promise, the architecture faces several challenges. Despite these challenges, its future remains bright."
after: A risk section states that the design has not been tested under region loss and that clock skew can expire all leases together.
annotation: This rule is the structural form of specific-over-generic (P5). Sections exist to meet the document's needs. An outline slot alone does not justify a section. The test applies P5's sentence test to sections. A section that survives a subject swap asserts nothing.

title: Epic titles state the strategic outcome
before: "Checkout improvements"
after: "Reduce checkout abandonment after recoverable payment failures"
annotation: An outcome title lets readers distinguish a strategic change from a topic or project container (P5).

title: User-journey task titles state the journey
before: "Fix expired cards"
after: "A buyer can retry checkout after replacing an expired card"
annotation: The title must preserve the journey's smallest useful account. A component or activity title hides the user outcome (P5, P6).

title: Engineering-only task titles state the technical outcome
before: "Refactor checkout events"
after: "Checkout events preserve order during payment retries"
annotation: Engineering-only work still needs an acceptance target. Activity labels such as "refactor" or "cleanup" do not supply one (P5, P6).

title: Subtask titles state the contribution
before: "Frontend work"
after: "Preserve entered billing data after an expired-card response"
annotation: A subtask is useful only when its contribution to the parent condition is visible without opening the document (P5).

title: Tasks declare both classifications
before: `Type: bug`, with no Outcome class
after: `Outcome class: user-journey` and `Change reason: defect-correction`
annotation: The two fields separate what accepts the work from why the work exists. One overloaded type cannot represent both decisions (P2, P7).

title: Defect corrections identify the violated contract
before: "Users dislike the current behavior, so this is a bug."
after: "Contract: Task T-18 requires saved billing fields after payment rejection. Evidence: recording R-4 shows those fields become empty."
annotation: Unwanted behavior is not necessarily a defect. The contract distinguishes restoration from a new product requirement (P6).

title: Engineering-only tasks identify their support
before: "This task has no user impact, parent outcome, or inherited invariant."
after: "Technical boundary: checkout event order. Supported invariant: Epic E-7 INV-3."
annotation: The required link prevents engineering-only classification from becoming a way to omit product or system purpose (P5, P6).

title: Epic invariants have stable identifiers
before: An unnumbered list of constraints that child tasks paraphrase independently.
after: "INV-2: A failed payment shall not delete entered billing data."
annotation: Stable identifiers let child work items inherit one exact property without copying wording that can drift (P2, P6).

title: Children preserve inherited invariants
before: INV-2 covers every failed payment, but one child preserves data only for expired cards.
after: A child cites INV-2 and verifies that every covered rejection preserves billing data.
annotation: An `epic` cannot ground its children when local acceptance silently reduces a shared constraint (P3, P6).

title: Epics remain strategic
before: The `epic` embeds T-18's path steps, local test cases, and implementation contribution.
after: The `epic` states INV-2 and links Task T-18 for the expired-card journey.
annotation: The `epic` grounds work. It does not replace the tactical documents that own independently acceptable outcomes and contributions (P8).

title: Tasks are independently acceptable
before: One task combines retrying checkout, exporting invoices, and changing account ownership.
after: "A buyer can retry checkout after replacing an expired card."
annotation: Independent acceptance is the tactical boundary between one task and several tasks under an `epic` (P6, P8).

title: Subtasks name one parent
before: `Parent tasks: T-18, T-21`
after: `Parent task: T-18`
annotation: A contribution with two parents has ambiguous scope, inheritance, and acceptance ownership (P6, P7).

title: Subtasks name one parent condition
before: `Supports the task definition of done`
after: `Parent completion condition: T-18 CC-2`
annotation: The condition is the subtask's complete reason for existing. A missing or multiple mapping makes its acceptance boundary unclear (P6, P7).

title: Independent outcomes use task
before: A complete user journey remains a `subtask` because the implementation is small.
after: A separately releasable account-recovery journey uses `task`, although its implementation changes one file.
annotation: Size, duration, repository count, and team count do not define the hierarchy. Acceptance independence does (P8).

title: Tasks summarize delegated sad paths
before: "Payment failures: see ST-4."
after: "SP-2: The bank times out. Checkout preserves billing data and offers retry. Owner: Subtask ST-4."
annotation: Delegation can move technical detail. It cannot remove user-visible behavior from the tactical acceptance contract (P3, P6).

title: Aggregate sad paths stay with the task
before: T-18 delegates the combined rollback path to the form subtask alone.
after: T-18 verifies rollback after the form saves data and the payment retry fails.
annotation: No one subtask can own behavior that appears only after several completion conditions interact (P6).

title: Technical hints do not carry normative content
before: "Technical hint: the implementation must preserve billing data for 30 days."
after: "Technical hint: the existing expired-card test fixture may supply the rejection response."
annotation: A reader may skip a hint. Normative content must remain in the exact acceptance contract (P3, P6).

title: Happy paths state the complete journey
before: "The buyer completes checkout."
after: "The buyer has an expired card. The buyer replaces it. Checkout retries payment and confirms the order."
annotation: The title compresses the journey. The happy path restores the complete acceptance sequence without requiring implementation steps (P6).

title: Sad paths state failure and recovery
before: "The retry can fail."
after: "The retry times out. Checkout reports the timeout, preserves billing data, and offers another retry."
annotation: A failure account is incomplete when it omits the product response, preserved state, or available recovery (P6).

title: Engineering success paths state the technical outcome
before: "Refactor the retry code and run tests."
after: "With event order recorded, enable retry. Verification confirms that all retried events retain their original order."
annotation: Engineering acceptance needs a reproducible transition and observation even when no user journey changes (P6).

title: Engineering failure paths state recovery
before: "Handle retry failures."
after: "If retry reorders an event, stop release. Keep the existing processor active and restore the recorded configuration."
annotation: A technical outcome is incomplete when its failure leaves system state or recovery unspecified (P6).

title: Simplification preserves exact meaning
before: "The new queue prevents checkout failures" as the plain rendering of a design that only bounds overload behavior below 20,000 requests per second.
after: "The new queue protects checkout from traffic spikes (exact design constraints in §4.2)." Section 4.2 limits the statement to a stated load range. Section 4.2 also defines the latency and loss invariants.
annotation: The two-layer model (§1.2) fails silently when a simplified statement loses exact content. A decision may lose a trade-off. A procedure may lose a precondition. A result may widen its scope. The rendering reads well but is wrong. Serves P3.

title: Simplified statements trace to exact statements
before: "In plain terms: stop if anything looks wrong." The statement has no pointer to the exact checks, threshold, or rollback boundary.
after: "In plain terms: stop the rollout if verification fails (exact checks and rollback boundary in Procedure §6)."
annotation: Traceability makes Rule 5.1.1 checkable. A reviewer compares the rendering against its target instead of searching for the target. Serves P3 and P7. A linter can flag simplified-claim markers without references. A human judges equivalence.

title: Define every non-baseline symbol at first use
before: "We minimize L(θ) by stochastic gradient descent." Neither L nor θ has been defined.
after: After admitting *model* and *training*: "Write θ for the model's stored numbers. Write L for the scoring function. L(θ) means the score for the model configured by θ."
annotation: A reader cannot expand an unknown symbol. Unlike an unknown word, the symbol cannot even be sounded out. The term ladder also applies to notation. Serves P4. A linter can flag symbols that appear before a defining sentence. A human judges definition quality.

title: One symbol, one meaning
before: α is the learning rate in §3 and the significance level in §5.
after: α is the learning rate everywhere in the document. The significance level is written out or receives a different symbol at admission.
annotation: Symbol reuse forces the reader to remember which local meaning applies. The assumed reader may choose the wrong meaning when it matters. Serves P2. Tooling can check the document's symbol table.

title: Notation table above six symbols
before: The same report defines all seven symbols across nine pages of prose with no table.
after: A capacity report defining λ, μ, Q, W, C, U, and R includes a notation table before the first analysis section.
annotation: In-prose definitions scale to a handful of symbols. Beyond that number, the reader needs an index to recover a definition without rereading. The threshold of six remains provisional. Serves P4.

title: Every displayed equation gets a plain-language reading
before: The same displayed equation is followed directly by "Optimization proceeds by stochastic gradient descent." No reading explains what L measures or why L matters here.
after:
Before the display, the document defines every symbol. N is the number of examples. The symbol i identifies one example. The expression x_i is that example's input. The expression y_i is its correct answer. The expression f(x_i) is the model's prediction. L is the average error. Σ means add the following expression for every i from 1 through N. The superscript 2 means multiply the difference by itself.
    L = (1/N) Σ_{i=1..N} (y_i − f(x_i))²
"This is the model's average error on the training data. For each of the N training examples, subtract the model's prediction f(x_i) from the correct answer y_i. Square each difference, so overshooting and undershooting both count as error. Then average the squared differences across all examples. Training, defined in §2, searches for parameters that make this number small. The rest of this section measures how that search behaves."
annotation: The assumed reader follows basic software concepts but may parse neither code nor mathematical notation fluently. The reading documents the equation. The reading also explains why the equation appears there. A reader may skip an unmotivated equation. Section 4.6 permits that skip only for bounded blocks, not load-bearing equations. Serves P3 and P4. A linter can flag displayed equations without adjacent readings. A human judges adequacy.

title: Keep inline math atomic
before: "Since L = (1/N) Σ_{i=1..N} (y_i − f(x_i))² < 0.05 after one epoch, we proceed to ablations."
after: "The error L falls below 0.05 after one pass over the data, as shown in Equation 2."
annotation: Complex inline math breaks the sentence's grammatical thread. Sentence length caps (§3.1) also become meaningless. Displayed equations receive a reading under Rule 5.3.1. Inline fragments cannot receive that reading. Serves P1. Rule 5.3.2 is the construct-specific override anticipated in §1.4(5).

title: Material statements carry a complete evidence record
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514; IEC 82079-1; APA JARS / NeurIPS checklist (research adaptation)
before: "The new queue fixes latency." The statement has no version, load context, baseline, evidence, invariant, evidential strength, uncertainty, or proposal status.
after: After admitting *p99* under §2.3: "For API v3, we replayed 12,000 requests/s. Verification confirms the proposed bounded queue keeps p99 latency below the existing 450 ms objective. The current implementation reached 710 ms. The proposed build reached 398–421 ms across five runs. Section 3 defines interface changes and the no-loss invariant. Section 6 links the harness and traces. The measured range reports run-to-run uncertainty. The design is proposed, not approved."
annotation: An incomplete exact item cannot be checked, reproduced, implemented, or compared. Context, alternatives, evidence, strength, uncertainty, and status make the item complete. Profile fields make each profile's exact items complete. Serves P6.

title: No naked percentages
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514; APA JARS (effect size + uncertainty, restated)
before: "Our method reduces latency by 18%."
after: "Latency fell 18% relative (from 340 ms to 279 ms median across 10,000 requests in the production replay)."
annotation: "Improved by 5%" can mean 61% → 66%. The phrase can also mean 61% → 64.05%. Headline numbers often travel without their context. Rule 5.4.2 applies the specificity principle (P5) to numbers.

title: Every citation resolves
before: A citation whose DOI resolves to an unrelated article, or whose URL does not resolve and has no archived copy.
after: "RFC 9110, *HTTP Semantics*, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html." The URL resolves to that RFC.
annotation: A valid-looking DOI that resolves elsewhere and a dead, unarchived link are hallucination signals, not ordinary link rot. Mechanical resolution checks run in §8.2. Serves P6.

title: Cited sources support the claim
before: Citing an architecture overview for a retry guarantee it never states.
after: Citing API contract §3.2 for "clients may retry this operation safely" when §3.2 specifies idempotent retry behavior.
annotation: Resolution (Rule 5.4.3) is necessary but insufficient. A real source may not support the claim for which it is cited. An unsupported citation is the harder-to-catch half of citation fabrication. The subject-matter-owner review (§8.4) checks support where that review tier applies.

title: Source counts are accurate
before: "Several studies report the same reversal (Kim 2024)."
after: "Two studies report the same reversal (Kim 2024; Osei 2025)."
annotation: Source-count inflation borrows authority the evidence does not have. Section 2.6 prohibits vague-attribution phrasing. Rule 5.4.5 covers the counted form. Serves P5 and P6.

title: Label axes, units, and series completely
before: A curve labeled "performance" over an unlabeled X axis.
after: After admitting *p99* and *logarithmic scale*: X axis "request rate (requests/s)," Y axis "p99 latency (ms)," legend naming the current and proposed queue, caption noting the logarithmic X axis.
annotation: An unlabeled axis makes the figure unfalsifiable. A hidden logarithmic scale makes the figure misleading. Serves P6.

title: The caption states the takeaway
before: "Figure 3: Queue latency."
after: After admitting *p99* under §2.3: "Figure 3: The proposed queue meets the 450 ms p99 invariant through 12,000 requests/s. Each point is the median of five replays. Bars show minimum and maximum."
annotation: Readers, especially skimming readers, read captions before body text. "Latency by load" only describes the artifact. "The proposed queue meets the latency invariant through 12,000 requests/s" informs the reader. Rule 5.5.2 applies §4.5's informative-heading rule to captions. Serves P5.

title: Figures stand alone for the assumed reader
before: The same timeline labeled only with internal codenames and unexplained alert abbreviations.
after: An incident timeline uses "request router," "database connection pool," and "rollback." All labels are assumed or admitted before the figure. The caption states: "Figure 3: Error rate recovered only after the router rollback. Increasing the connection pool did not change the error rate."
annotation: Figures travel: they are extracted into slides, reviews, and summaries without their body text. A figure that depends on unadmitted vocabulary breaks exactly when it travels. The admitted-terms-only constraint is checkable against the document's ladder state (§8.2). Serves P4.

title: Strength and authority language comes from the table only
before: "The obviously superior queue clearly guarantees that no jobs can be lost."
after: "We propose a bounded queue. Verification confirms that the prototype meets the no-loss invariant in the fault cases in Table 4."
annotation: With a closed vocabulary, the reader can distinguish verified behavior, observation, interpretation, adopted decision, proposal, and hypothesis. With an open vocabulary, every adverb is a negotiation. Intensifiers on top of table phrases smuggle strength the evidence or approval status never earned. Serves P6 and P7.

title: Strength matches the evidential standard
before: "Verification confirms the dependency caused the timeout." Only correlation in five replay runs supports the claim.
after: "We observed the timeout on all five replay runs. The evidence indicates that the dependency limit is involved. We did not vary that limit."
annotation: The table works only when the mapping is honest. "Verification confirms" backed by an unrun test violates calibration. "We decided" for an unapproved proposal also violates calibration. Both phrases belong to the permitted vocabulary. The subject-matter owner (§8.4) audits this mapping where that review tier applies. Serves P6.

title: Admit ladder-required statistical concepts before use
before: "The improvement is statistically significant (p < 0.05)" in a document that never admits p-values.
after: "The gap (4.2 points) is larger than the seed-to-seed spread of either model (at most 0.8 points across 5 runs)."
annotation: "Significant" is the sharpest trap in the set. The assumed reader hears "large." The writer means "unlikely under a null hypothesis the reader has never met." Serves P2 and P4.

title: Headline statistical results use bare concepts
before: "The fine-tuned model outperformed the baseline (paired t-test, p = 0.003)" as the only statement of the result.
after: "Across 5 runs, the fine-tuned model beat the baseline every time, by 3.9 to 4.6 points (mean 4.2). Using the paired t-test and p-value defined in §3, p = 0.003."
annotation: The two-layer model also applies to statistics. The exact formulation remains available to the expert. The assumed reader receives the finding in familiar vocabulary. Serves P3 and P4.

title: Reports include the applicable checkability statement
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514; IEC 82079-1; NeurIPS checklist / ML Reproducibility Checklist (research adaptation)
before: A system report says only "tests passed," or a research paper scatters settings across footnotes without stating data availability or required resources.
after: A system report's "Verification" section names the tested build, replay input, environment, commands, pass thresholds, and access gap. A research paper's "Reproducing this work" section covers data, code or procedure, resources, key settings, and gaps.
annotation: A claim that cannot be repeated or independently checked remains dependent on the authors' environment and access. The profile-specific form makes checkability explicit without forcing an experiment-oriented statement onto a system report. Serves P6.

title: The statement reads in assumed-reader vocabulary
before: "See Appendix B for hyperparameters and infrastructure details."
after: "Reproducing this work: We trained on the public C4 text dataset, about 750 GB, available from its maintainers. Training code and configurations are in our internal repository `forge/plateau-study`. The reported runs used 64 H100 GPUs for roughly 9 days total across all experiments. The most important settings are the 0.001 learning rate and the data order. Appendix B gives the learning-rate schedule. We fix data order with the seeds in Table 5. The evaluation questions are private. A reproducer would need to substitute a comparable question set. Appendix C describes how we built our question set."
annotation: The assumed reader uses the statement to assess independent checking. A pointer where an answer should appear defeats the section. An appendix or linked harness extends the statement. The appendix or harness does not replace the statement. Serves P3 and P4.

title: One definition of done per work item
before: The `task` has separate Product done, Engineering done, and Quality done sections.
after: One `task` has one Definition of done containing conditions CC-1 through CC-3.
annotation: Separate product, engineering, and quality definitions create competing closure authorities. One slot makes completion auditable (P2, P7).

title: Completion conditions state the pass test
before: "CC-1: Handle expired cards correctly."
after: "CC-1 passes when checkout retains all five billing fields after test response `expired_card`."
annotation: A condition without an observation or method cannot support acceptance without reviewer invention (P6).

title: Task conditions have stable identifiers
before: Three unnumbered checkboxes are referenced as "the first two items" by child documents.
after: `CC-1`, `CC-2`, and `CC-3` identify three distinct completion conditions.
annotation: A stable identifier lets one `subtask` map to one condition without copying or renaming the acceptance statement (P2, P7).

title: Subtask evidence verifies the parent condition
before: "The form component tests pass."
after: "Test V-4 verifies T-18 CC-2 by comparing all five billing fields before and after the rejection."
annotation: A local implementation result does not establish parent acceptance unless the evidence reaches the parent's exact condition (P3, P6).

title: Tasks verify integrated behavior
before: T-18 checks each component alone and never retries payment through the complete journey.
after: After CC-1 and CC-2 pass, T-18 retries payment and verifies that saved billing data reaches the new request.
annotation: Local conditions can pass while their combined user journey or technical outcome fails (P6).

title: Closed subtasks do not close the task
before: Automation closes the `task` when the final child closes, although integrated retry fails.
after: Every child is closed. The `task` closes after its happy path and aggregate sad paths pass.
annotation: Tracker status is not evidence that the independently acceptable outcome passes its integrated checks (P6, P7).

title: Epic completion verifies outcome and invariants
before: The `epic` closes when its task list is empty, with no outcome or invariant check.
after: The `epic` records its outcome measure and verification for INV-1 through INV-3 after all in-scope tasks close.
annotation: Child completion does not establish the product-level outcome or preservation of the constraints that grounded those children (P6).

title: Every completion condition must pass
before: CC-1 passes and CC-2 fails. The `task` closes because one path works.
after: CC-1 and CC-2 pass. Integrated check V-6 passes. The `task` closes.
annotation: A definition of done requires all its conditions. One failed condition leaves the work item's closure contract unsatisfied (P6, P7).

title: Anchor analogies in assumed-reader vocabulary
before: For the same pod audience: "The rollback boundary is like an aircraft's V1 speed." The anchor is outside the declared baseline. The document has not admitted the anchor.
after: For a software engineering pod: "A request queue is like a waiting line. Both hold items until processing. Unlike a physical line, software can process several queued items at once."
annotation: An analogy explains only if its anchor is already understood (P4). The shared baseline and selected genre overlay define available anchors. Neither supplies domain knowledge; other anchors require admission.

title: State the breaking point
before: "A circuit breaker works like a conditional guard around a dependency call."
after: "A circuit breaker works like a conditional guard around a dependency call. Unlike the guard, the circuit breaker remembers recent failures and changes state over time."
annotation: The reader cannot tell which anchor properties transfer. The writer can identify those properties (P3). An analogy without a breaking point silently exports false properties. The "except" clause is the price of using the analogy. A linter can flag analogy markers without an adjacent "except," "unlike," or "but" clause. A human confirms the substantive break.

title: At most one analogy per concept
before: "Rollback is like rewinding a recording, or perhaps like restoring a version-control commit while the service traffic is a river." Three anchors compete.
after: "Rollback restores the last compatible database schema and then replays queued writes. Rollback does not reverse messages already delivered to external systems."
annotation: Stacked analogies force the reader to reconcile multiple anchors with the concept. The document never states that reconciliation (P4). A concept needing more support requires a definition or worked example, not another analogy.

title: Central mechanisms get a worked example
before: "Deploy version 2, verify success, and roll back if needed." The procedure asserts its central state transition without tracing the transition.
after: In a procedure: "Before the change, production runs version 1. Deploy version 2 to the test environment. Submit order 123. Verify order 123 appears in the order list within 30 seconds. After verification passes, deploy version 2 to production. Otherwise, stop and run rollback step R1."
annotation: The assumed-reader test (§1.2) fails most often at mechanisms the writer understood too well to walk through. A worked example is the only device the reader can check themselves against (P4). A peripheral mechanism **may** rely on definition alone.

title: Examples carry no incidental complexity
before: "Start with the full production event, including 40 unrelated metadata fields. Follow the event through every analytics export." The extra fields and systems do not help explain redaction.
after: In a privacy explanation: "Start with one log entry containing an email address and a request identifier. Show the redaction step replacing the email address while retaining the identifier used for debugging."
annotation: Every incidental detail is a candidate explanation the reader must rule out (P4). Two nodes show a failover state transition as well as a 40-node fleet. Three timeline events show evidence ordering as well as thirty.

title: Examples use realistic values
before: "Device A receives value `foo` and returns value `bar`."
after: In a hardware procedure: "Discharge a 5 Ah test battery at 25 °C and 1 A for 30 minutes. The example uses the procedure's cell type and units at a shorter duration."
annotation: Placeholder values include "foo," "widget," and x₁…x₉. Such values force the reader to map the example back to reality. The worked example should perform that mapping (P5).

title: Intuition is bounded and labeled
before: "Requests then enter the queue. Loosely, the queue absorbs any traffic spike, which is why overload cannot reach the database." The informality is inline and unbounded. The passage states the informal explanation as a guarantee.
after: > **[Intuition — backpressure]** Think of the bounded queue as a buffer between a fast producer and a slow consumer. Unlike an in-process buffer, the queue may reject producers. Producers must handle that response.
annotation: The boundary tells the reader and linter where precision is suspended (P3). Unmarked informality in main text blurs the sentence's layer.

title: Exact content does not live only in intuition blocks
before: > **[Intuition — compatibility]** Old clients can use field `name` until 30 September. After that date, the service returns only `display_name`. The requirement and date exist nowhere else in the design.
after: > **[Intuition — compatibility window]** Keeping both response fields for one release resembles briefly supporting two function signatures. Unlike local callers, network clients upgrade independently. Section 4.2 gives the exact compatibility invariant and removal date.
annotation: Rule 6.3.2 extends ISO/IEC Directives Part 2's "notes shall not contain requirements" to every profile. Exact content hidden in an intuition block escapes evidence rules (§5.4, §5.6). The content may also escape required subject-matter review (§8.4). Block content must derive from the exact layer or remain removable without harm. A linter can flag calibrated phrases and normative keywords inside intuition blocks. A human must find unphrased exact content.

title: Main text survives block removal
before: An intuition block introduces a "safe window." The procedure later says "deploy during the safe window" without defining dates or checks in main text.
after: main text defines the compatibility invariant, an intuition block offers the two-signature picture, and later sections use only the exact invariant.
annotation: The block boundary promises that its content is optional (P4). A later sentence cannot depend on content found only in an intuition block. Such content is load-bearing and belongs in main text. Rule 6.3.3 applies §4.6's skip-coherence requirement to intuition blocks.

title: Diagram structures that prose cannot carry
before: "The gateway sends accepted jobs to the queue. The worker drains the queue while writing state to the database. During overload, the gateway rejects jobs before enqueue." No diagram shows these interactions.
after: A design RFC shows the gateway, queue, worker, and database as labeled boxes with request and failure paths. The prose walks the diagram.
annotation: Prose serializes information. Structure is parallel (P4). Three interacting components create more pairwise relations than one sentence can hold in working memory.

title: Every diagram is referenced from the text
before: A state diagram floats above the procedure. No step or sentence mentions the diagram.
after: "Figure 2 shows the failover states and the verification path used in steps 4–7."
annotation: An unreferenced diagram forces the reader to integrate content without guidance. Otherwise, the diagram is decoration (P7). The reference tells the reader when to leave the prose.

title: Diagram labels use admitted terms only
before: The same diagram labels the state "L7 quiesced" when neither "L7" nor "quiesced" has been admitted for the profile's assumed reader.
after: A diagram referenced in §2 labels its middle state "traffic drained," a term admitted in §1.
annotation: A reader reads a diagram as a unit. One unadmitted label can make the whole picture illegible to the assumed reader (P2, P4). The check uses the document's ladder state at the referencing sentence. Section 2.3 applies the same check to prose.

title: Diagrams carry alt text
before: `alt="diagram"`.
after: `alt="Requests flow from gateway to queue to worker. Overload rejection occurs before the queue."`
annotation: Some tools that display governed documents may not render images. Alt text also tests whether the diagram has one stateable point.

title: Repeat verbatim or not at all
before: "Recall that rollback is the safe way back to the old system." (A new, weaker framing wearing a recall marker.)
after: "Recall: the rollback boundary is the last step after which the previous version can be restored without data repair." (Identical to the §2 definition.)
annotation: Varied restatement forces the reader to check whether the variation is a new statement (P2). Identical wording makes the repetition instantly recognizable as recall, not news. Rule 6.5.1 generalizes STE's consistent-repetition principle from terms to statements.

title: Recall distant definitions at reuse
before: After more than 2,500 intervening words, "the replay harness" reappears bare. The assumed reader must re-derive its meaning.
after: "The replay harness (§2.3: the tool that sends a recorded request set to a test deployment) reproduces the timeout in 92% of runs."
annotation: The ladder admits a term once, but admission does not ensure retention (P1, P4). The 2,500-word threshold represents five Rule 4.8.1 pages. The threshold is provisional. Section 8.3 reader-testing results calibrate it.

title: Recap the ladder at part boundaries
before: A recap is woven into opening prose as new content and explains rollback in fresh words. The recap fails Rule 6.5.1. Without a marker, the recap reads as news.
after: "Recall: *rollback boundary* means the last step after which the previous version can be restored without data repair. *Verification query* means the read-only query that confirms the new version serves current data."
annotation: A recap at the boundary lets a returning reader re-enter without rereading (P1). The recap remains ordinary main-flow content, not a §4.6 bounded block. `Recall` is not one of the closed bounded-block labels.

title: No hollow summaries
before: "In summary, this section reviewed the incident timeline and discussed the major contributing factors."
after: An incident-analysis section ends with its last bound: "The traces establish when retries began. Retention expired before the first connection failure. The trigger therefore remains unknown."
annotation: A hollow closing paragraph repeats content the reader just read. Common openers include "In summary," "Overall," and "Taken together, these results." This pattern is opposite to Rule 6.5.2's distant recall. The pattern is also a clear structural symptom of generic prose (P5). A conforming document deletes a closing paragraph that adds nothing. A closing paragraph remains substantive when it adds a consequence, bound, or forward pointer. Linters flag the opener phrases. A human confirms deletability.

title: Boundary material is required
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514; IEC 82079-1; NeurIPS Paper Checklist (research adaptation)
before: A decision record whose only compatibility limit appears in a footnote beside one rejected option.
after: A decision record puts version and dependency limits in **Context**. The decision record puts option-specific security and reversibility trade-offs in **Alternatives**. The decision record puts accepted failure and revisit conditions in **Consequences**.
annotation: The aggregation point for §7.2's in-line caveats must exist before it can aggregate (P6). Short profiles may keep the section brief, but no profile is exempt from stating where its primary outcome stops.

title: State the scope of validity
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514; IEC 82079-1; NeurIPS Paper Checklist / Model Cards (research adaptation)
before: "This procedure restores the service." The statement has no environment, version, dependency, capacity, privilege, or verification boundary.
after: "This procedure is verified for service versions 4.8–4.10 on Kubernetes 1.32, at up to 200 active jobs per worker. The procedure assumes operator access to the recovery vault. The procedure is not verified for the managed-cloud deployment, whose rollback API differs."
annotation: Scope is part of an exact statement (P6). Readers often assume wider compatibility, load tolerance, trust boundaries, data coverage, or external validity than the evidence establishes. Boundary disclosure prevents that silent widening.

title: Disclose known failure modes and adverse effects
before: The expired-access failure appears in test logs but nowhere in the procedure or its boundaries.
after: "If vault access expires after step 6, rollback cannot restore the old encryption key. New writes remain readable. Records written before rotation become unavailable until access is restored. No data is deleted."
annotation: Failure modes are findings (P6). Omitting an observed failure converts a known boundary into a reader's surprise. Omitting the failure's effect hides risk needed for a design, decision, procedure, or deployment choice.

title: Disclose what was not tested or verified
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514; NeurIPS Paper Checklist / Datasheets for Datasets (research adaptation)
before: A design validated in one region at 2,000 requests/s says "supports failover at production scale" and names no untested boundary.
after: "We did not test cross-region failover or dependency versions before 3.6. We also did not test sustained load above 12,000 requests/s or recovery after step 9's point of no return."
annotation: A list of everything untested would be infinite. The dangerous gap contains untested conditions the primary outcome invites the reader to assume (P6). Rule 7.1.4 turns the checklist assumptions item into a disclosure.

title: Disclose data limitations
before: "The logs show the worker caused the outage." The statement omits provenance, retention gaps, clock bounds, transformations, and privacy handling.
after: "Gateway logs came from all six affected hosts, but worker debug logs had seven-day retention and expired for the first 18 minutes. Host clocks were synchronized within 200 ms. The export removed request bodies because they contain personal data."
annotation: Data flaws propagate silently into every conclusion derived from the data (P6). A research claim inherits its dataset's limitations. An incident conclusion inherits log retention and clock quality. A capacity decision inherits traffic-sample coverage limits.

title: Plausible boundary gaps are explicit
before: A design names its tested version but says nothing about the visibly relevant cross-region condition.
after: "Data scope: not applicable. This decision uses no collected or generated data. Cross-region behavior: untested."
annotation: Silent omission makes an unknown boundary look unlimited. An explicit state distinguishes deliberate exclusion from a missed disclosure. "Plausibly relevant" avoids an infinite inventory of impossible conditions.

title: Caveats attach to their claims
before: Step 8 says "Promote the replica," while the 2-second precondition appears only in the procedure's later boundary material.
after: "Run step 8 only while replica lag is below 2 seconds. Above that value, promotion can lose acknowledged writes. Section 7.1 collects the full recovery boundary."
annotation: Readers quote claims and act on decisions and procedure steps where those statements appear (P6). An unreached or distant caveat does not bound the statement in the reader's mind. For the same reason, "disconnect power first" belongs at the affected step, not only in a preface.

title: Boundary material aggregates, it does not replace
before: The procedure's boundary material is the first and only mention of the promotion limit.
after: The 2-second promotion limit appears in step 8 and again with the other caveats under Scope and Failure and escalation.
annotation: The aggregate view supports a reader assessing the whole document. The in-line caveat supports the reader at the point of use (P6). Each location has a separate job. Neither location replaces the other. Moving a caveat only to aggregated material hides the caveat from its point of use. The warning-placement rule prevents that failure.

title: Separate observation from interpretation
before: "Database connections reached the configured maximum at 09:14 UTC. The dependency upgrade therefore caused the outage." The observation and causal interpretation share one chunk.
after: The split incident passage below.
annotation: Observation and interpretation have different evidential standards (§5.6). Mixing them lets an interpretation borrow certainty from its adjacent timestamp, trace, test, or measurement (P6). A linter can flag chunks that mix measurement syntax with interpretive phrases. A human confirms the distinction.

title: Speculation only in marked blocks
before: "A credential refresh probably started the connection churn." The statement appears unmarked in main text. Retained evidence does not support the statement.
after: > **[Speculation — first connection failure]** We speculate that a credential refresh started the connection churn, but the relevant authentication logs had expired.
annotation: Speculation records the authors' best guess for future work. Speculation has value only when readers cannot mistake it for a finding (P3, P6). The standard block boundary identifies its status. Rule 4.6.3 keeps the main text coherent after removal of non-load-bearing speculation.

title: Speculation uses the speculative tier
before: "**[Speculation — credential refresh]** The record shows that a credential refresh started the churn." "The record shows" is a verified-tier phrase.
after: > **[Speculation — credential refresh]** We hypothesize that the unrecorded credential refresh started the connection churn.
annotation: "The record shows" or "we decided" reintroduces certainty or authority inside a speculation block (P2). One table governs evidential-strength and decision-authority language (§5.6). The block label and its phrases must agree.

title: Extrapolations name the target setting
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514; NeurIPS Paper Checklist / APA JARS (research adaptation)
before: "The rollback procedure works everywhere."
after: "For the managed-cloud deployment on service version 4.11, the evidence indicates that the same rollback sequence may work. The deployment's different snapshot API must satisfy the preconditions in §3."
annotation: "This works in production" is a claim about an unstated universe (P5, P6). Naming the target converts an unbounded extrapolation into a checkable one and forces the writer to distinguish what is established from what is expected.

title: Beyond the boundary, drop evidential strength
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514; NeurIPS Paper Checklist / CONSORT (research adaptation)
before: "Verification confirms the procedure on versions 4.8–4.11." Version 4.11 was never tested or otherwise established.
after: "Verification confirms the procedure on versions 4.8–4.10. The evidence indicates, but does not establish, that the procedure works on 4.11. Version 4.11 was unavailable during verification."
annotation: Evidence earned in one setting supports, at most, an interpretation or proposal about another (P6). Strength must decrease at the established boundary. Section 5.6 supplies fixed vocabulary for that decrease. A linter can flag verified or observed phrases near settings absent from the evidence record. A human confirms the boundary.

title: Checklist is generated, not authored
before: A reviewer copies the `research-paper` checklist, deletes statistics by hand, and calls the result a procedure checklist.
after: The checklist header records ITWS 0.6.0-draft, profile `procedure`, tier `reviewed`, and the Annex C revision from which it was generated.
annotation: A hand-maintained checklist diverges from the rules the first time a rule changes (P7). Generation makes the checklist correct by construction.

title: Four self-check passes
before: "`itws-lint` passed, so self-check is complete." No author checked the partial and human-only rules.
after: The author of a `decision-record` completes all four passes. The passes include the applicable alternatives, consequences, status, and boundary checks.
annotation: Core still requires substantive human checking. Lint alone cannot judge operational definitions, coherent structure, exact interfaces, or evidence quality. Four passes with one concern each keep that check usable (P7). Reviewed and publication tiers reuse the completed checklist instead of making reviewers rediscover basic defects.

title: Regeneration on rule change
before: A rule is reclassified recommended → mandatory and existing generated checklists still list it as optional.
after: Adding `technical-report` to a rule's `Profiles` line triggers checklist regeneration before the specification release.
annotation: Section 0.8 permits rules to change between versions. Profile and tier metadata also determine applicability. A stale checklist silently checks the wrong specification or document class.

title: Lint gate
before: "The linter is noisy. Readers can ignore the linter." Errors remain for review or release.
after: A core `investigation-log` links a clean `itws-lint` run pinned to ITWS 0.6.0-draft and profile `investigation-log`.
annotation: Machine-checkable violations are the cheapest to find and the most embarrassing to ship. The lint gate is part of core, so short-lived documents receive it even when their minimum tier has no independent reviewers.

title: Severity maps to rule class
before: All custom checks report warnings "to be safe."
after: The §3.10 copula-avoidance check enforces a mandatory rule and reports an error. A recommended density-budget heuristic reports a warning.
annotation: Section 0.4.2's three classes lose meaning when tooling flattens them. A blocking warning teaches writers to ignore severity. A nonblocking error does the same.

title: Version-pinned checking
before: A 0.6.0-draft `procedure` is checked against the latest lists and the `research-paper` profile inferred from its references section.
after: `itws-lint --spec 0.6.0-draft --profile design-rfc queue-design.md` loads the 0.6.0-draft lists and the `design-rfc` rule set.
annotation: Sections 0.4.4 and 0.8 guarantee checking against the cited version. Profile applicability decides which rules enter that check. A linter that always runs the latest lists or guesses a profile breaks both guarantees.

title: Machine checks do not close human gates
before: "CI is green, ship it." No self-check is recorded.
after: Lint passes. The author still completes all four self-check passes. A reviewed-tier procedure then receives both required independent reviews.
annotation: Most mandatory rules are `partial` or `no` on machine-checkability. The linter finds phrase-list and ordering violations. The linter does not find every blurred interface, unsafe rollback, unsupported causal claim, or misleading explanation. Treating lint as human verification is the failure mode P7 prevents.

title: Publication gate
before: "The reader-proxy reviewer said it reads fine." The proxy is not an independent test participant. No release checks are recorded.
after: A `research-paper` release record includes reviewed-tier approvals and a new independent participant's successful result teach-back. The record also includes resolved citations and artifacts. The checklist was generated for ITWS 0.6.0-draft.
annotation: Publication claims both independent comprehension and release readiness. The reader test catches a plain layer that changes the primary outcome. Release checks catch a correct draft with stale metadata, broken evidence, inaccessible artifacts, or missing approvals.

title: Participant sampling
before: The reader-proxy reviewer, who has read three drafts, is the test participant.
after: A quality assurance specialist from an unrelated pod matches the `procedure` baseline. They have never seen the system change. They use the final procedure to walk through the task.
annotation: The test measures what the document teaches, not what the participant already knew or absorbed in drafting, review, or project discussion. Contaminated participants pass documents that fail real readers.

title: Protocol and pass criteria
before: The participant can summarize why the maintenance matters but skips the precondition and invents a restart as rollback.
after: For a procedure, the participant waits until replica lag is below 2 seconds. The participant performs the verification query. When the query fails, the participant chooses rollback R1.
annotation: A universal research-result test would not measure every profile's primary outcome. Such a test would miss procedure execution, decision recovery, and safe incident interpretation. The profile task ties the acceptance test to the document's job. The task retains two common failure directions: boundary creep (§7.4) and status or strength creep (§5.6).

title: Reader-test failures are recorded
before: "Reader test failed." The record states no misstatement or failed action.
after: "Participant omitted the point of no return in step 6 and chose rollback after step 8."
annotation: The misstatement or failed action is the finding: it points at the section that failed to teach and gives the revision a testable target.

title: Failed documents are revised and independently retested
before: The same participant rereads the revised draft and supplies the answer discussed after the first test.
after: A participant misses a rollback boundary. The author moves the boundary next to the affected step. A second qualified participant tests and passes the revision.
annotation: Revision closes the recorded comprehension gap. A new participant tests the document, not the first participant's memory of the session.

title: Reviewed tiers use two independent roles
before: The RFC author reviews it "wearing both hats," or a core `decision-record` is rejected solely because it did not recruit two reviewers.
after: A service owner signs a reviewed `design-rfc` for interfaces, invariants, evidence, and boundaries. A product designer from another pod signs for the plain layer.
annotation: The two layers fail in opposite ways. The owner can fill gaps from domain knowledge, but the proxy cannot judge technical correctness. Splitting the roles runs both acceptance tests without imposing two reviewers on core-tier documents.

title: Subject-matter-owner scope
before: The owner copyedits sentence length and skips the interface invariant because "the proxy has the checklist."
after: The owner flags a procedure whose rollback step is unsafe after the schema migration even though the draft calls rollback available throughout.
annotation: These checks require knowing what the domain permits and what the evidence supports. Each overlay `README.md` gives its profile a concrete owner review focus, such as interfaces and invariants for a `design-rfc`, mechanism fidelity for an `explanation`, or integrated acceptance for a `task`. The focus narrows the owner's attention. The focus does not reduce the owner review scope above.

title: Assumed-reader proxy scope
before: The proxy lets "fence the old primary" pass because the database team knows its meaning. The declared assumed reader does not know the phrase.
after: The proxy flags "quiesce L7" in a procedure because neither term is assumed or admitted. The state transition is required to execute the critical path.
annotation: The proxy's value is disciplined ignorance: they read as the declared Annex B baseline, not as themselves. A proxy who fills gaps from project knowledge silently passes documents that fail the real reader.

title: Findings cite rules
before: "this section feels weak" with a requested rewrite and no rule.
after: "§3.10 violation: replace 'serves as the backbone of' with 'is'."
annotation: Rule plus violation is the complete enforcement model (P7, §1.3). The model ends arguments and reveals gaps. A recurring opinion without a citable rule is a candidate for the next specification version.

title: Deviation requires a recorded waiver
before: "Everyone knows Section 3 does not follow the ladder. The deviation is fine."
after: a §4.8 density-budget violation in a survey section, waived with justification and an approver, linked from the conformance statement.
annotation: An undocumented deviation is indistinguishable from an unnoticed deviation. Silent exceptions damage the entire rule set (P7). The self-exclusion prevents Rule 8.5.1 from nullifying itself.

title: Waiver content
before: a repository-wide "waived: §2.3" note with no location, approver, or expiry.
after: the filled template below.
annotation: A waiver missing its location or approver cannot be audited. A waiver missing its scope silently becomes permanent policy.

title: Generated artifacts satisfy the generation contract
before: A committed `rules.jsonl` names ITWS 0.5.1-draft while the front matter reads 0.6.0-draft, and no command reproduces the file.
after: `python3 tools/itws_compile.py --check` reports no difference, and `manifest.json` records ITWS 0.6.0-draft with a hash for every file under `spec/`.
annotation: A checklist, a rule index, and a navigation catalog are only trustworthy when a reader can regenerate them and compare bytes. Recorded source hashes turn a stale artifact into a detected error rather than a silent one. Determinism keeps a regeneration diff readable, so a reviewer sees the rule change instead of reordering noise.

title: Stale artifacts are rejected, not reused
before: The validator notices the changed hash, prints a warning, and still reports `pass`.
after: The validator stops and reports which source file changed after generation.
annotation: Section 0.4.4 checks a document against its declared version. An artifact generated from different source silently checks a different specification. Rejecting the run turns that mismatch into a visible failure, which is the outcome Rule 8.2.3 already requires of every version-pinned input.

title: Validation reports one of four states
before: The same document reports `pass` because the linter found nothing.
after: A `decision-record` with a clean lint run and no recorded self-check reports `needs_review`, and the report names the missing gate.
annotation: A two-state report forces every unfinished check into either a false pass or a false failure. Rule 8.2.4 already says a clean machine run does not close a human gate; separate states let a tool say so instead of implying the opposite. The `blocked` state also gives a pipeline somewhere to put a missing fact, so it reports the gap rather than inventing content.

title: Agent-authored judgments cite their support
before: "Lines 41–48 are evidence." No rule, no span, and no state.
after: "Lines 41–48 are an evidence chunk (§4.1, Rule 7.3.1); state: proposed."
annotation: Rule 8.4.4 already requires a review finding to cite its rule. A machine-authored classification needs the same discipline for the same reason: a judgment without a citation cannot be checked, argued with, or revised. The judgment state keeps an uncertain reading available instead of forcing a premature choice.

title: Colliding rewrites are reported, not merged
before: The tool applies the later patch and silently discards the earlier one.
after: The patch report lists both proposals, the shared span, and the shared `term-ledger` write, and it applies neither.
annotation: Parallel repairs are safe only where they touch disjoint text and disjoint ledgers. Two rewrites that both rename one artifact, or both edit one paragraph, produce a document that no reviewer approved. A tool can detect the collision mechanically. Only a reader can decide which rewrite survives, because the decision depends on meaning.
